short: The Senate's triple-bayed monument to victory over Maxentius, dedicated on Constantine's tenth anniversary.
full:
The Senate built the Arch of Constantine beside the Colosseum between 312 and 315 CE, dedicating it on 25 July 315 to mark ten years of Constantine's reign and his defeat of the rival emperor Maxentius at the Battle of the Milvian Bridge in October 312. The largest surviving Roman triumphal arch, it has three bays and stands over 20 metres high, its attic inscribed with a claim that Constantine had won by the prompting of a divinity, deliberately unspecified between the pagan Sol Invictus and the Christian god he was moving toward.

Much of the decorative sculpture was reused from monuments of earlier emperors, Trajan, Hadrian and Marcus Aurelius among them, their heads recut to Constantine's likeness. Older scholarship read this as decline in the sculptors' skill; more recent assessment treats it as deliberate, positioning Constantine within a lineage of celebrated predecessors at a moment of political transition. The arch has stood substantially intact since antiquity and remains the closest thing to a full architectural record of that transition from the pagan to the Christian empire.
